Data analysis report
COVID-19 daily figures
Cleaning, exploring and testing 100 days of reported cases, deaths and recoveries
5 March to 12 June 2020  ·  Source: covid.json  ·  Python, pandas, statsmodels, matplotlib

What the file contains: running totals of confirmed cases, deaths and recoveries, the number of active cases, and the new cases and new deaths reported each day.

Assumption
The file doesn't name the country. The dates and numbers match South Africa's early outbreak: the first case on 5 March 2020, and the first deaths on 27 March, the day the national lockdown started. I work on that assumption, and it only matters in one place: the timeline is split using South Africa's lockdown levels. Every other result depends on the numbers alone.

Questions this report answers¶

1Is the data clean and consistent, and what has to be fixed before it can be analysed?
2How fast did cases and deaths grow, and did growth change when lockdown levels changed?
3Are there reporting patterns, such as quiet weekdays or late batches, that could mislead a reader?
4What do the numbers say about the risk of dying after a confirmed infection?
5If nothing changed, where was the curve heading?

1First look at the raw file¶

Before changing anything, I load the file exactly as it is, with every value kept as text, so nothing gets converted behind my back.

int 84 95 84 22 78 100

What needs fixing
  • Mixed types. Five of the six number columns mix integers and text. Any maths on them would fail or, worse, silently treat '1 139' as a word. Only Daily deaths never passes 999, so it stays numeric.
  • Untidy column names. Daily deaths has two spaces and different capitalisation from the others.
  • Dates are text in YYYY/MM/DD form, so they don't sort or plot as dates.
  • First row. On 5 March the running total is 1 but Daily Confirmed Cases is 0. That first case has to count as new on some day, and there is no earlier row, so it belongs to 5 March.

2Cleaning¶

The clean() function in covid_analysis/data.py fixes each problem above. Nothing was dropped, filled in or estimated.

Step What it does Why
1 Rename columns to short snake_case names Consistent, typo-proof names in the code
2 Parse date as a real date Correct sorting, gaps can be checked, proper time axis on charts
3 Strip spaces from numbers and convert to integers '1 139' becomes 1139. Conversion is strict: anything that isn't a number raises an error instead of becoming a blank
4 Sort by date, drop duplicate dates Safety net; this file needed neither
5 Set new cases on 5 March to 1 Makes daily cases add up to the final total

3Consistency checks¶

Clean types don't prove the numbers are right, so I test the rules the numbers should obey.

  • dates run every day, with no gaps or repeats
  • running totals never go down
  • active = confirmed − deaths − recovered on every day
  • daily figures equal the change in the running totals
Data quality checks
check days_failing passed
No missing values 0 ✓ Pass
No duplicate dates 0 ✓ Pass
No gaps between dates 0 ✓ Pass
No negative numbers 0 ✓ Pass
Totals never go down 0 ✓ Pass
Active = cases - deaths - recovered 0 ✓ Pass
New cases = change in total cases 0 ✓ Pass
New deaths = change in total deaths 0 ✓ Pass
What this shows
Every check passes. Once the formatting is fixed, the numbers agree with each other on every day. So any odd pattern later on comes from how the data was reported, not from typing errors in this file.
Caution
One thing these checks can't catch is how often a column was updated. Section 5.6 shows that recoveries were updated in batches rather than daily, which limits how far those numbers can be trusted day to day.

4New columns¶

add_features() adds the columns used in the rest of the analysis.

Column Meaning
phase Lockdown level on that date: Before lockdown (to 26 Mar), Level 5 (27 Mar to 30 Apr), Level 4 (May), Level 3 (from 1 Jun)
weekday Day name, used to look for reporting patterns
new_recovered Change in total recoveries from the day before
cases_7d, deaths_7d 7-day rolling averages, which smooth out day-to-day noise and weekday effects
growth_7d Average daily growth of total cases over the past week, on a log scale
doubling_days Days for total cases to double at that growth rate: ln(2) / growth
cfr Case fatality rate: deaths / confirmed cases
resolved_cfr Deaths / (deaths + recoveries), counting only cases whose outcome is known
recovery_share, active_share Share of confirmed cases that have recovered, or are still active

What this shows
Mean daily cases (619) sit far above the median, and the standard deviation is bigger than the mean. That's what an exponential curve looks like: most days are small, and a few late days are very large. Plain averages over the whole period are misleading, so the rest of the analysis works per phase, on a log scale, or with rolling averages.

5Visual exploration¶

Ten charts, each answering one question about the data.

5.1 New cases per day¶

What this shows
  • Cases climb quickly in March, flatten through April, then rise steadily from May and much faster in June.
  • Single days jump around a lot (see the dip in early April and the spike on 4 June). The 7-day average is a much better guide to the trend than any one day.
  • The low on 28 March (17 cases, after 243 the day before) is almost certainly a reporting gap, not a real drop.

5.2 Total cases on a log scale¶

On a log scale, steady exponential growth is a straight line, and a steeper line means faster growth. That makes it the right way to compare growth across phases.

What this shows
The curve is made of straight sections with a sharp bend at the start of lockdown. Before lockdown, total cases doubled roughly every 2 days. From Level 5 on, doubling time stretched to 12 to 15 days and stayed there through Levels 4 and 3. The dashed lines fit very well (R² of 0.98 or above), so a constant growth rate per phase is a fair summary.

5.3 Doubling time over time¶

What this shows
Doubling time jumped from under 3 days to around 20 days within the first week of lockdown, then settled at 11 to 14 days from late April.
Caution
The jump happens too quickly to be caused by lockdown alone. People infected just before lockdown would still have been showing symptoms and getting tested for a week or more afterwards. Part of this early change is probably about testing, such as who qualified for a test and how fast labs reported. The file has no testing numbers, so the two can't be separated.

5.4 Deaths per day¶

What this shows
Deaths begin on 27 March and follow the same shape as cases, a few weeks later: low through April, rising through May, and climbing fast in June. With small counts in April, single days are very noisy.

5.5 Outcomes of confirmed cases¶

What this shows
By 12 June, of 61,927 confirmed cases, 35,008 (57%) had recovered, 25,565 (41%) were still active and 1,354 (2.2%) had died. Active cases were still rising steeply, so the load on the health system was still growing at the end of the data.

5.6 How recoveries were reported¶

Data quality issue
This is the biggest data quality issue in the file. Recoveries were not reported daily. On 55 of the 100 days the total stayed the same, followed by large jumps (for example from 45 to 410 on 10 April). Only from mid-May were they updated almost daily. What that means:
  • new_recovered should not be read as "people who recovered that day".
  • active_cases depends on recoveries, so it is overstated between updates and drops when a batch arrives.
  • Any rate that uses recoveries (the resolved fatality rate below) is unreliable before mid-May.

6Statistical analysis¶

Seven questions, each answered with a test suited to time-series data, and each with its limits stated.

6.1 Each phase in numbers¶

Daily cases and deaths per lockdown phase
  Start End Days Cases added Mean daily cases Median daily cases Max daily cases Deaths added Mean daily deaths Max daily deaths
Before lockdown 05 Mar 26 Mar 22 928 42.2 13.5 218 0 0.0 0
Level 5 27 Mar 30 Apr 35 4,719 134.8 99.0 354 103 2.9 14
Level 4 01 May 31 May 31 27,036 872.1 767.0 1,837 580 18.7 52
Level 3 01 Jun 12 Jun 12 29,244 2,437.0 2,484.5 3,359 671 55.9 82
What this shows
  • Level 3 ran for only 12 days but added 29,244 cases, nearly as many as the previous 88 days combined (32,683).
  • Deaths followed: 671 in those 12 days against 683 in all the days before.
  • The median day under Level 5 had 99 new cases. Under Level 3 it had 2,485.

6.2 Growth rate of total cases per phase¶

Method
For each phase I fit a straight line to the log of total cases against time. The slope is the daily growth rate, converted to a doubling time with ln(2) / slope. The 95% confidence intervals come from the slope's standard error.
Growth of total cases, fitted per phase
  Days Daily growth Doubling (days) 95% CI low 95% CI high R²
Before lockdown 22 38.3% 2.1 2.0 2.3 0.980
Level 5 35 4.8% 14.8 14.4 15.3 0.990
Level 4 31 5.8% 12.2 12.0 12.3 1.000
Level 3 12 5.6% 12.8 12.2 13.5 1.000
What this shows
Once lockdown began, the doubling time went from 2.1 days to 14.8, about seven times longer (daily growth fell from 38% to 4.8%). Growth then picked up a little under Level 4, and the intervals for Level 4 and Level 3 overlap.
Caution
These intervals are narrower than they should be. Running totals carry every earlier day inside them, so the points are far from independent. The next test deals with that.

6.3 Did the growth rate really change between phases?¶

Method
A stronger test is a segmented regression on the 7-day average of new cases instead of the running total, fitted across the whole period:

log(new cases, 7-day avg) = a + b·day + (change in slope at each phase start)

Each phase gets its own slope, and the model tests whether each one differs from the one before. Days next to each other are correlated, so ordinary standard errors would be too small. I use Newey-West (HAC) standard errors, which allow for that correlation over a 7-day window.
Model coefficients (slope changes on the log scale)
  Coefficient Std. error z p-value 95% CI low 95% CI high
const -0.185 0.358 -0.517 0.605 -0.887 0.516
Before lockdown 0.205 0.027 7.456 0.000 0.151 0.259
Level 5 -0.174 0.036 -4.775 0.000 -0.246 -0.103
Level 4 0.036 0.014 2.588 0.010 0.009 0.063
Level 3 -0.029 0.015 -1.873 0.061 -0.059 0.001
Growth of daily new cases in each phase
  Daily growth 95% CI low 95% CI high Doubling (days) p (change vs previous)
Before lockdown 22.7% 16.3% 29.5% 3.4 –
Level 5 3.1% 1.1% 5.2% 22.5 0.000
Level 4 6.9% 5.8% 8.1% 10.4 0.010
Level 3 3.9% 1.7% 6.1% 18.2 0.061
What this shows
  • Before lockdown, daily new cases grew about 23% a day (95% CI 16% to 30%), doubling every 3.4 days.
  • Level 5 cut this to about 3% a day. The change is highly significant (p < 0.001), even with the stricter standard errors.
  • Level 4 saw growth more than double, to about 7% a day (p = 0.010). That fits with restrictions easing on 1 May, though wider testing in May would also push the numbers up.
  • Level 3: growth in the first 12 days was lower, at about 4% a day, but with so few days the change is not statistically significant (p = 0.061). It's too early to say Level 3 changed anything.
Caution
The 7-day average reacts a few days late, and policy changes take one to two weeks to show up in confirmed cases. The phase boundaries are calendar dates, so read these as "growth while each level was in force", not as the precise effect of each level.

6.4 Is there a weekday reporting pattern?¶

Method
Many countries report fewer cases after weekends, because labs and offices slow down. I divide each day's count by a centred 7-day average, so 1.0 means an ordinary day. I then compare weekdays with a Kruskal-Wallis test, which doesn't assume the ratios are normally distributed. Only days from April are used, when counts were large enough for ratios to mean something.
Kruskal-Wallis H = 7.86, p = 0.249
Ratio of each day's cases to its weekly average
  Mean ratio Median ratio Std. dev. Days Std. error
Monday 0.920 0.997 0.201 10 0.064
Tuesday 0.851 0.817 0.205 10 0.065
Wednesday 0.965 0.897 0.318 9 0.106
Thursday 1.090 1.016 0.293 9 0.098
Friday 1.083 1.119 0.185 9 0.062
Saturday 1.030 1.040 0.385 10 0.122
Sunday 1.077 1.045 0.253 10 0.080
What this shows
Tuesdays (0.85) and Mondays (0.92) come in a little below average, and Thursday to Sunday a little above, which fits a weekend lag in testing. But the differences are small next to the day-to-day noise, and the test finds no significant weekday effect (p = 0.25). With about 10 weeks of data the test can only pick up a large effect, so a small one could still be there. The ratios from one week also share the same average, so they aren't fully independent, and the p-value is a guide rather than an exact figure. Either way, it supports using 7-day averages rather than single days.

6.5 How deadly was a confirmed infection?¶

Method
There are two common ways to measure fatality while an epidemic is still running, and they pull in opposite directions:
  • Naive CFR = deaths / all confirmed cases. This understates risk, because many recent cases haven't had an outcome yet.
  • Resolved CFR = deaths / (deaths + recoveries). This overstates risk early on, because deaths are often recorded faster than recoveries. Here, recoveries were also reported late (section 5.6).

The true value usually ends up between the two. Intervals use the Wilson method for proportions. They only cover sampling error; the reporting delays behind the gap between the two measures are a much bigger source of uncertainty.

Case fatality rate on 12 June
  Deaths Out of Rate 95% CI low 95% CI high
Naive (deaths / cases) 1,354 61,927 2.19% 2.07% 2.30%
Resolved (deaths / (deaths + recovered)) 1,354 36,362 3.72% 3.53% 3.92%
What this shows
On 12 June the naive CFR was 2.19% (95% CI 2.07% to 2.30%) and the resolved CFR was 3.72% (95% CI 3.53% to 3.92%).

The resolved CFR peaks near 29% in early April. That isn't real: deaths had started but almost no recoveries had been recorded yet. Once recoveries were reported regularly, it settled near 4%. The naive CFR crept up from under 1% in March to just over 2%, as deaths caught up with the cases behind them.

Deaths trail diagnosis by a couple of weeks. So another view is to divide this week's deaths by the cases from some days earlier:

Deaths in the last week divided by cases from earlier weeks
  Deaths / earlier cases
Cases from the same week 2.41%
Cases from 7 days earlier 3.14%
Cases from 14 days earlier 4.89%
Cases from 21 days earlier 6.76%
What this shows
Against cases from two weeks earlier, deaths come to about 4.9%, more than double the naive figure. This doesn't prove the true rate is that high. It shows how much the headline 2.2% depends on cases still being early in their illness.
Note
These are case fatality rates, not infection fatality rates. Many infections were never tested, so the share of all infected people who died would be much lower.

6.6 Do changes in cases predict deaths? A correlation trap¶

Correlating daily cases with daily deaths gives a very strong result:

Pearson r between daily cases and daily deaths: 0.91 (p = 2.6e-39)
Why this number is misleading
r = 0.91 looks impressive, but most of it is the shared upward trend: any two things that grow over the same 100 days will correlate. To get past that, I take the day-on-day change in the log of each 7-day average, which removes the trend, and check whether a change in cases is followed by a change in deaths some days later. The grey band shows what pure chance produces. It widens at longer lags, because fewer pairs of days are left to compare.
What this shows
After removing the trend, most lags show nothing beyond chance. Two rise above the band: 11 days (r = 0.31) and 17 days (r = 0.47). A 17-day delay would fit the two to three weeks from diagnosis to death often reported for COVID-19, but there are good reasons to be careful:
  • I tested 22 lags, so one or two crossings are expected by chance alone.
  • The simple p-value at 17 days is 0.002, but it assumes independent points. Daily changes in deaths swing back and forth from one day to the next, so the true p-value is larger.
  • The lags on either side are near zero or negative, where a real effect would usually show a broad peak.

I read this as a hint of a roughly 2.5-week delay, not a finding.

The main point: the raw r = 0.91 should not be used to claim that cases "predict" deaths.

6.7 Where was the trend heading?¶

Method
I fit a log-linear trend to the last 21 days of total cases and carry it forward two weeks. This is a "nothing changes" line, not a forecast.
Recent daily growth: 5.6%  (R² = 0.999)
Where the trend points after 14 days
Date Projected cases 95% PI low 95% PI high
26 Jun 2020 133,369 128,692 138,216
What this shows
At the growth rate of the last three weeks, about 5.6% a day, total cases would reach about 133,000 by 26 June, more than double the 61,927 on 12 June.
Caution
The shaded interval looks tight, but it only covers random scatter around the trend. It does not cover changes in testing, policy or behaviour, and those are what actually move an epidemic curve. Day-to-day errors are also correlated, which makes the true uncertainty larger than shown.

7What the data is saying¶

The main conclusions, in order of how much weight they can carry.

01The data is reliable in structure but uneven in reporting
Once the number formatting was fixed, every consistency check passed. The weak spot is recoveries, reported in batches until mid-May, which distorts active cases and any rate that uses recoveries.
02Lockdown coincided with a sharp, statistically clear slowdown
Before 27 March total cases doubled about every 2 days; afterwards it took 12 to 15. Growth in daily new cases fell from about 23% to 3% a day (p < 0.001). Part of the early change is probably due to testing, because it happened faster than lockdown could act on infections.
03Growth never stopped
In every phase, daily new cases kept growing at 3% to 7% a day. That still means doubling every 10 to 23 days, which is how Level 3's 12 days produced almost as many cases as the 88 days before them.
04Growth picked up when Level 4 began
From about 3% to 7% a day (p = 0.01). Level 3 shows a lower rate so far, but 12 days is too few to tell it apart from Level 4.
05Between about 2% and 4% of confirmed cases had died
The 2.2% headline is very likely an underestimate, because recent cases hadn't yet had time to end in death or recovery.
06Single-day numbers are noisy
There's a mild, non-significant weekday pattern and some obvious reporting gaps. Use 7-day averages for any decisions.
07The trend was still rising
Active cases and the 7-day average of deaths were both at their highest on the last day, and the recent trend pointed to cases doubling again within about two weeks.

8Limitations and next steps¶

What this data can't tell us, and what would make the analysis stronger.

Limitations
  • No testing data. More confirmed cases can mean more spread or more testing, and this file can't tell them apart.
  • Country assumed. If it isn't South Africa, section 6.3 needs different phase dates; the rest still holds.
  • Reported date, not event date. Figures may trail the real test or death by days.
  • National totals only. Regions could be on very different paths.
  • Short final phase. Level 3 has only 12 days.
Next steps
  • Add daily testing numbers and analyse the positivity rate.
  • Add the provincial breakdown to see whether one region drove the national curve.
  • Estimate the reproduction number (Rt) with a proper epidemiological model.
  • Extend the data past June 2020 to check the projection against what actually happened.
